title: Namangan drivers gather over methane station queues
location: Chorsu Square near the Namangan city administration, Namangan, Uzbekistan
organizer: No organizer identified; the report describes the action as spontaneous and says no leader had formed demands to take to the administration.
participants_original: At least 50 drivers, as reported by Ozodlik.
threshold_50_evidence: Ozodlik explicitly reports at least 50 drivers gathered. Its brief embedded video excerpt is not treated as a crowd count.

title.summary: The Ozodlik article describes drivers gathering in central Namangan.

start_date.summary: The report dates the gathering to January 13, 2021 and places it between 1 and 2 p.m.

start_precision.summary: The article gives a calendar day for the gathering.

end_date.summary: One unnamed driver said the group stood for one or two hours and then dispersed; the reported start time places this on January 13.

end_precision.summary: Physical departure is reported for the same day, but the exact end time is unavailable.

location.summary: The source places at least 50 drivers at Chorsu Square by the Namangan city administration building.

scope.summary: The report describes a local gathering in Namangan; it provides no evidence of a coordinated national action.

organizer.summary: A driver characterized the action as spontaneous, with no organizer/leader to formulate demands.

demands.summary: Drivers expressed dissatisfaction with methane-station queues, but the report says they had not formulated demands; no demand category is assigned.

participants_original.summary: The article's reporter says at least 50 drivers gathered.

participants_min.summary: The explicit lower bound is 50 drivers.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The source explicitly states at least 50 drivers; the limited embedded clip is not used to replace that report.

protester_violence.summary: The report does not describe violence by participants; silence is coded unknown.

state_response.accommodation.summary: No response to a formed protest demand is reported; comments made to the reporter about supply pressure do not establish accommodation.

state_response.arrests.summary: The article reports no event-specific arrests; absence in this account is not explicit absence.

state_response.beatings.summary: No event-specific beating is reported; value remains unknown.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: One driver says participants dispersed after one or two hours; the article does not attribute their departure to state force or an order.

state_response.ignore.summary: The account says the group had not formed demands or a leader; a receptionist's comments to a journalist do not establish government avoidance of a received demand.

state_response.killings.summary: A driver death in a fuel queue on January 10 is described as a prior incident, not a killing during or in response to this gathering; this event's response remains unknown.

state_response.shootings.summary: No event-specific shooting is reported; value remains unknown.

eligibility.summary: Occurrence, date, local public location and a 50-person lower bound are supported, but no state-directed demand is documented.

notes: Ozodlik's own report is the substantive source. Mediazona's search result (S023) explicitly attributes its account to Ozodlik and is not independent corroboration. The article separately mentions a January 10 death in a fuel queue and a January 11 car fire; neither is assigned to this gathering as a casualty or response. The embedded clip is a brief excerpt; no visual attendance count is inferred.
open_questions: Does the grievance about gas-station queues constitute a demand directed to Uzbekistan's government or its service policy under the original coding rules, despite the report saying the drivers had not formulated demands?
No physical end time is available; confirm whether the attributed one-to-two-hour dispersal is sufficient for the day-level end field.

title: Altyaryk refinery workers protest planned layoffs and work stoppage
location: Altyaryk branch of the Fergana Oil Refinery, Altyaryk District, Fergana Region, Uzbekistan; exact gathering point is described as the street beside the plant
organizer: No organizer identified in the captured accounts; participants are refinery employees
participants_original: The Labour Mission report headline describes hundreds of workers; no exact attendance count is given in the captured event-specific text.
threshold_50_evidence: The Labour Mission report headline describes hundreds of workers participating in the protests. The refinery's workforce size and the number said to risk layoffs are not used as attendance counts; exact assembly bounds remain unknown.

title.summary: The reports describe Altyaryk refinery employees protesting job-cut plans and the plant's work stoppage.

start_date.summary: Both reports date the beginning of the workers' protest to January 10, 2021. RFE/RL retrospective S030 also dates the refinery action to January 10; this is same-family reporting, not independent confirmation.

start_precision.summary: The source accounts provide a calendar day for the reported start.

end_date.summary: Labour Mission and Eurasianet describe recurring activity through reports dated January 18-19; RFE/RL retrospective S030 says the protest lasted more than a week from January 10. None gives the last physical gathering date, so the end remains unknown.

end_precision.summary: Although the RFE/RL retrospective describes a duration exceeding one week, it does not date the final physical gathering; no exact closing date is inferred.

location.summary: The accounts locate the action at the Altyaryk refinery; the worker cited by Labour Mission says participants blocked the street beside the plant.

scope.summary: The sources describe repeated actions by Altyaryk branch workers, not a national or multi-site gathering.

organizer.summary: No organizer or union is identified in the captured accounts.

demands.summary: Workers objected to planned layoffs, reduced work and wages, and plant inactivity; the Labour Mission title and attributed worker statements include requests for work and oil. The categorized labor demand is clear, but its state target is not.

participants_original.summary: The Labour Mission article headline characterizes the protest as involving hundreds of workers.

participants_min.summary: No precise minimum is provided. The plant's reported 900 employees and the 800 said to risk losing work are not participant counts.

participants_max.summary: No upper bound is reported; Eurasianet's figure of about 200 workers moved to company headquarters is not turnout at the Altyaryk action.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The report headline uses the qualitative quantity 'hundreds' for the protesting workers, which supports the threshold; no precise interval is inferred.

protester_violence.summary: The captured text does not describe violence by protest participants; value remains unknown.

state_response.accommodation.summary: A refinery spokesperson denied planned layoffs and a filmed manager promised no closure, but these are company statements and not evidence of an own-state response; value remains unknown.

state_response.arrests.summary: No event-specific arrest is reported in the captured accounts; absence is not explicit absence.

state_response.beatings.summary: No event-specific beating is reported; value remains unknown.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: A worker attributed to Ozodlik says police arrived at the place and dispersed protesters. This is an attributed claim about dispersing people, not merely traffic or police presence; the originating account is RFE/RL-family reporting.

state_response.ignore.summary: No explicit state avoidance or refusal of a government-directed demand is documented; value remains unknown.

state_response.killings.summary: No event-specific killing is reported; value remains unknown.

state_response.shootings.summary: No event-specific shooting is reported; value remains unknown.

eligibility.summary: Eurasianet describes Jizzakh Petroleum as a joint venture involving the state-owned Uzbekneftegaz and Gazprom, but workers' reported complaints target company management. The captured accounts do not establish an explicit demand to Uzbekistan's government or its policy.

notes: The Labour Mission page is a distinct report, but it attributes a protester's main account to Ozodlik; its body reports recurring after-work street blockades and that police arrive and disperse protesters. Eurasianet independently interviewed an FNPZ spokesperson and an anonymous employee, but explicitly attributes the event start and footage to Ozodlik. RFE/RL-family search-result versions S037 and S038 are same-origin discovery leads, not independent confirmation, and were not opened under the coordinator's hold. Jizzakh Petroleum's joint-venture ownership does not by itself prove that the protest demanded government action. Plant staffing and the 200 employees reportedly moved to Fergana headquarters are not assembly counts. Daily actions do not establish uninterrupted physical presence or a last day; end date remains unknown. RFE/RL analysis S030 also reports an Altyaryk protest beginning January 10 and lasting more than a week; it is within the same publisher family and does not establish a precise last physical gathering date.
open_questions: Were the January protests explicitly directed at the Uzbekistan government, a public policy, or only refinery/Jizzakh Petroleum management? Keep pending_state_target until evidence resolves this.
The Labour Mission headline says hundreds, but no exact attendance or independently assessed visual count is available.
The captured reports do not establish the last physical gathering date; check February for a related continuation without assuming every-day presence.
No organizer or participant violence is established in the captured accounts.
Russian-language source material has not received independent human language review.

title: Paxtakor women block highway over household gas and electricity interruptions
location: Paxtakor District, Jizzakh Region, Uzbekistan; highway segment not identified
participants_original: No crowd size is reported. Ozodlik later says nine protesters from this episode were tried: five received five-day administrative detention and four warnings; this legal count is not used as attendance.
threshold_50_evidence: The article confirms a group of women blockaded a highway but gives no number; whether at least 50 people assembled remains unresolved.

title.summary: RFE/RL and the Tashkent Times describe mostly women from Paxtakor blocking a road over gas and electricity shortages.

start_date.summary: The article says local officials met with the women on January 11 and places the blockade before that date’s presidential visit.

start_precision.summary: The report gives the calendar day January 11.

end_date.summary: The women ended the highway blockade after the local government secured immediate delivery of one ton of cheap coal; the report places this sequence on January 11.

end_precision.summary: The report documents physical end of the blockade on January 11 but gives no exact time.

location.summary: Both reports identify Paxtakor district, Jizzakh Region; the exact road segment is not named.

scope.summary: A local group of women in Paxtakor blocked a highway; no wider coordination is reported.

organizer.summary: Neither the RFE/RL report nor its cited summary identifies an organizer.

demands.summary: The women protested lack of household gas and electricity. The Tashkent Times reports residents said supplied liquefied gas and coal were only enough for cooking. The sources do not state that cheap coal was their demand and the grievance does not clearly fit the seven available demand categories.

participants_original.summary: The Tashkent Times reports social-media footage showed mostly women residents; neither opened account gives a numerical count.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The source confirms an assembly and road blockade but provides no headcount to establish the 50-person threshold.

protester_violence.summary: The account does not describe participant violence; silence is coded unknown.

state_response.accommodation.summary: RFE/RL reports a meeting and immediate one-ton coal delivery secured by local government; Tashkent Times reports the provincial first deputy governor and other officials spoke with residents and promised gas provision within a week. The promise is not proof gas was restored.

state_response.arrests.summary: Ozodlik reports that nine participants were tried in two proceedings after the January 11 blockade: five men were sentenced to five days of administrative detention and four women received warnings. This is an event-linked state detention response; these counts are not turnout.

state_response.beatings.summary: One detainee alleged that people he understood to be regional police officers insulted and struck him in custody; Jizzakh regional police explicitly denied psychological pressure or physical force. The competing accounts are preserved and the response remains unknown pending review.

state_response.crowd_dispersal.summary: Local authorities urged the women to unblock the highway, an explicit request to end the road blockade. The article says the blockade ended after coal delivery and does not attribute the departure to a forced clearing.

state_response.ignore.summary: Tashkent Times reports provincial and other officials arrived, spoke with residents and promised gas within a week; RFE/RL reports local officials met with the women. The state did not ignore this gathering.

state_response.killings.summary: Neither opened account reports event-specific killings; value remains unknown.

state_response.shootings.summary: Neither opened account reports event-specific shooting; value remains unknown.

eligibility.summary: The later report documents nine prosecuted participants and a direct public-service grievance with local-government engagement; the total assembly size remains unknown and the 50-person threshold is still pending.

notes: The January 12 RFE/RL Uzbek Service article (S059) reports that a group of women in Paxtakor blocked a highway over lack of household gas and electricity on January 11. Local authorities met with them and urged them to unblock the highway ahead of a presidential visit; the blockade ended after the local government secured immediate delivery of one ton of cheap coal. The article does not give attendance, exact road segment or organizer. It does not say the women requested coal or that gas/electricity were restored. The utility-service grievance does not map clearly to the seven available categories, so demands remains empty pending review. The linked Ozodlik and AMP versions are same-story service versions, not independent confirmation. The opened Tashkent Times report S056 is another publication about the same event; it cites Khududgaz Jizzakh and social-media footage, so independent reporting is not assumed for the official-response details. It says officials promised gas provision within a week; fulfillment is unverified. A January 26 Ozodlik follow-up S064 reports two administrative proceedings after the blockade: five men received five-day detention and four women warnings. One detainee alleged that regional police personnel beat him during custody; Jizzakh regional police denied force or pressure. The allegation and denial conflict, so state_response.beatings remains unknown. The nine legal cases are not used as attendance.
open_questions: How many people were present, and did the gathering meet the 50-person threshold?
Which demand category, if any, should represent a household gas/electricity service grievance under the original coding procedure?
Was the service issue a public-policy failure or a complaint directed to a utility provider? The local-authority meeting supports engagement but does not identify the service operator.
No exact hour or road segment is reported.
The promised gas delivery within one week is not verified as completed.
A detainee alleged a beating in custody while Jizzakh regional police denied it; the competing accounts have not been independently resolved.
